claims.text: Physically synthesized multi-element near-equiatomic nanoparticles have a critical temperature separating a kinetically stable mixed state from an unstable segregating state.
Below the critical temperature, configurational entropy and atomic-size mismatch produce high diffusion barriers and sluggish atomic kinetics.
Above the critical temperature, thermal energy overcomes the diffusion barriers and causes rapid diffusion, elemental segregation, and phase separation.
Physically synthesized near-equiatomic CoNiCuFeCr or similar nanoparticles can begin with homogeneous elemental distributions and fine, controlled grains.
Iteratively calibrated MC+MD simulations and in situ high-temperature TEM can jointly monitor diffusion and structural evolution versus temperature.
The proposed tests cover 473–1923 K and include inert, reducing, and oxidizing atmospheres.
Atomic diffusion rates and spatial elemental distributions mediate the effect of operating temperature on nanoparticle structural integrity.
Entropy-induced diffusion barriers can maintain a uniform elemental distribution during thermal annealing.
Atomic-size mismatch is an intrinsic cause of the proposed high diffusion barrier.
Accelerated atomic migration above the threshold causes surface segregation and eventual phase separation, compromising chemical and structural stability.
Below the critical temperature, the nanoparticles will exhibit minimal diffusion, uniform near-equiatomic composition, and stable morphology.
Above the critical temperature, diffusion coefficients will increase markedly and simulations and TEM will show segregation and phase demixing.
At the lower-temperature baseline, diffusion remains sluggish and the initially homogeneous structure is preserved.
The mechanism is most applicable to physically synthesized nanoparticles having typical grain sizes and defect densities.
Synthesis route, particle size distribution, microstructure, and reactive environment can alter diffusion rates and shift the effective threshold temperature.
The exact threshold and diffusion-rate values depend on calibration between simulations and experiments.
Failure to observe a marked increase in diffusion or segregation between 773 and 1173 K, or retention of homogeneity well beyond that range, would refute sluggish-diffusion control of stability.

contradictions.description: The boundary and uncertainty fields allow the threshold to shift with synthesis, size, defects, atmosphere, and calibration, whereas the falsification rule treats absence of a transition in 773–1173 K as refutation. A null result in that interval could instead indicate a shifted threshold, so the stated test is not unconditionally decisive.
